props.title: The Runaways
props.initialSlug: Teen rock rebels shake up '70s music scene

sections.content: The Runaways (2010) captures the gritty rise and fall of the groundbreaking all-girl rock band with raw teenage energy. Kristen Stewart and Dakota Fanning deliver electric performances as Joan Jett and Cherie Currie, diving deep into the 1970s punk scene when female rockers were revolutionary. The film follows similar beats to Almost Famous (2000) and Control (2007), but through a distinctly feminine lens that explores exploitation and empowerment in equal measure. Director Floria Sigismondi brings her music video background to create a visceral portrait of youth rebellion.

sections.content: The film sits in a vital space between celebration and cautionary tale, much like Sid and Nancy (1986) and Last Days (2005). While it showcases the thrill of creative liberation and musical rebellion, it doesn't shy away from the darker elements of the music industry in the 1970s. Michael Shannon's portrayal of manipulative manager Kim Fowley exposes the predatory aspects of the business, echoing similar themes in 20 Feet from Stardom (2013) and Amy (2015).

Beyond the music, The Runaways excels at capturing the specific cultural moment of late-70s Los Angeles. Like Boogie Nights (1997) and Once Upon a Time in Hollywood (2019), it recreates an era when the California dream was crashing into darker realities. The film's exploration of gender dynamics and sexual identity, particularly through Joan Jett's character, was ahead of its time, predating later music biopics like Bohemian Rhapsody (2018) in tackling these themes. sections.content: The film stands out in the male-dominated landscape of rock biopics, joining rare company with films like Prey for Rock & Roll (2003) and Her Smell (2018). It tackles the unique challenges faced by women in rock, from sexual objectification to industry dismissal, while never losing sight of the pure artistic drive that pushed The Runaways to break barriers. The authentic portrayal of female friendship and rivalry adds depth rarely seen in rock films.
